name: Sara Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a junior operator on a factory line that folds and glues paper flour bags. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check the fold-plate setting. A sealed bag that stands up straight is satisfying; clearing glue from the feeder is slow work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner does electrical repair callouts. We have two school-age children and a mortgage, with about two months of expenses saved. I earn typical factory pay and there are some similar plants nearby. I never use AI tools; I keep the bag checks on a paper card by the feeder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the bag crew a clever order list is fine, but the forming machine still needs somebody to catch a crooked paper seam. A customer carrying flour will notice a weak bottom long before an office report does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn the usual operator wage and my partner has regular electrical repair work. We have two months of expenses put by, two children and a mortgage, and there are some other factories within reach. If AI stays small, our income looks steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep feeding paper rolls and checking the first bags after the fold plates are set. The lead will show me the plate adjustment again on our next paid changeover; I'm still learning it. I don't use AI and don't plan to start just to write notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I know what needs doing on the next shift, and the family bills have a wage behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the seam check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Friday I found three bags with the seam glued too high, so we stopped and moved the plate before filling the pallet. That was a hand and eye check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you handle a variable repair week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I look at the mortgage and school costs each payday. We don't promise a new savings amount until we know what the electrical repair week actually paid.

say: **Paper bags** still need physical seam and bottom checks.
A quicker **order list** cannot repair a badly set fold plate.
think: Our two **current wages** cover the mortgage in the mild case.
Two months of **savings** and some nearby plants give a modest buffer.
do: **Keep** feeding paper rolls and checking each first bag.
**Practise** the fold-plate setting with the lead on paid time.
feel: **Calm** about familiar factory work and current household pay.
S0.quote: A customer carrying flour will notice a weak bottom long before an office report does.
fieldNote: Sara **never uses AI** and prefers physical checks taught by the lead operator.
Her **moderate cushion** and two current wages support calm while orders remain stable.

steps.text: Keep feeding paper rolls and checking first bag seams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that AI may book paper and schedule deliveries before it folds a bag. I want the manager to keep enough paid minutes for the first-bag check when the office sends more orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buying desk may change, but my hands-on work still needs doing and my partner repairs electrical faults in person. Our own income seems safe for now. I dislike new screens, though I can learn a mechanical setting when the lead shows me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor to write checking time into the new shift schedule and keep my paper record of first-bag faults. I'll practise the fold plate with the lead during a paid changeover, then wait for real evidence before accepting a shorter target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a faster schedule, not expecting a lost household wage yet. I don't want a rush to make a weak seam somebody else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you give the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the manager the last two bags that split at the glued bottom and how long a safe plate correction took. That gives a number for paid checking time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the schedule removes checking time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office sets a target without that time, I'd tell the shift lead before the run starts. A bag count is no use if the first pallet has to be scrapped.

say: **AI buying** may speed the office before hands-on bag forming changes.
The **first-bag check** needs paid time on any faster schedule.
think: Our own **wages look safe** while repair and bag work remain physical.
A rushed **production target** could make seams fail.
do: **Ask** supervisor to retain paid first-bag checking time.
**Keep** paper fault records and practise fold plates with the lead.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed checks while household income remains secure.
S1.quote: A bag count is no use if the first pallet has to be scrapped.
fieldNote: She asks for **paid checking time** through the supervisor, without claiming collective action.
Her **resistance to AI** remains; she relies on a proven mechanical setting and paper record.

steps.text: Keep paper seam-fault record and practise fold plates
Compare actual first-bag check time before accepting shorter target

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028 could plan our paper orders, and capable robots around 2031 could feed and fold bags. I'd tell my family that training for real work matters more than a speech about everyone adapting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the physical line work. If our crew is reduced, two months saved would cover only a short gap in my wage, and my partner's repair pay varies with bookings. There are some factories nearby, but none owes me a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the manager for a written crew plan. If a local plant posts a safe packing or machine role at enough regular pay to cover the mortgage, I'll apply when my hours are cut. If our factory offers a funded, paid-time practical setter apprenticeship with an actual supervised place, I'll enrol, although I would need the trainer beside me at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real wage cut, but I can ask about paid work and learn a machine face to face. I won't spend the mortgage money on an unoffered course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the apprenticeship teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprenticeship should show me a stopped feeder, a locked guard and how to clear a bad glue line without reaching into a moving press. I would need practice on a locked bag feeder, not an online clip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How might a different shift work at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister lives nearby and could collect the children if I took a different shift. I would ask her only after a real posted job and its hours were on paper, not for a vague factory rumour.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may plan paper orders before robots fold bags around 2031.
Adults need **paid practical apprenticeships** tied to real work.
think: At **48**, reduced line hours could strain the mortgage after two months saved.
Nearby **factory openings** and family help are possibilities, not guarantees.
do: **Ask** manager for a written bag-crew plan this week.
**Apply** for posted safe local factory work if hours fall and pay suffices.
**Enrol** in paid setter apprenticeship if an actual funded supervised place opens.
feel: **Anxious** about possible line-wage loss with some options.
S2.quote: I would need practice on a locked bag feeder, not an online clip.
fieldNote: She would accept **face-to-face practical training** while refusing to treat an enquiry as enrolment.
The **job application** requires cut hours and a safe posted local role at sufficient regular pay.

steps.text: Ask manager for written bag-line crew plan
Apply for posted safe local factory role if hours cut, pay sufficient
Enrol in setter apprenticeship if funded paid supervised place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI comes in 2031 and capable bag robots around 2034, I'd tell people we have five years to teach workers on real machines. A course needs an adult trainer and a paid place, not only a password.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots can fold bags. Our children will be older, but we may still owe on the mortgage and need both wages. Five years gives me time to qualify for another line if it pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep earning on the bag line and add a new amount to savings from full pay months after bills. If a nearby factory offers a recognized machine-setting course with covered fees, paid release and guarded practice, I'll enrol next year. Once qualified, if bag shifts fall, I'll apply to posted local setter jobs only if the hours and safe duties fit our family and the regular pay covers costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about income when robots reach the floor, but the years let me learn a setting without throwing away today's wage. My partner and I can make choices from real offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a practical test involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise setting a fold plate on an isolated feeder and making ten bags whose bottoms hold a load. The trainer needs to inspect ten sealed bags before I run a full pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unfunded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the course is unfunded, we cannot use the mortgage reserve for it. I would keep the paid line while looking for a place that covers both training time and fees.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes orders before robots fold bags around 2034.
A **paid adult trainer** should teach guarded machine settings.
think: At **51**, I still may need two wages for the mortgage.
A **recognized qualification** helps only with a real safe job at workable pay.
do: **Keep** bag-line work and add new savings after bills.
**Enrol** in recognized setting course if fees and paid guarded practice covered.
**Apply** to posted local setter work after qualification if hours fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about later wages, with a longer paid learning route.
S3.quote: The trainer needs to inspect ten sealed bags before I run a full pallet.
fieldNote: She begins **new saving** only from future full pay, without relabelling the existing reserve.
Course and **application** keep funded time, guarded practice, qualifications, safe local duties and sufficient pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full bag-line pay after bills
Enrol in setting course if fees and paid guarded practice covered
Apply for posted safe local setter job if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could run paper orders, and capable robots around 2039 could fold bags. I'd tell the family that ten years lets us prepare, but I won't treat a future machine as a reason to leave honest work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots arrive. The children will be grown or nearly grown, but that does not erase our mortgage or the need for a wage. Two months saved now is a start, not a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the current line job and put new savings from full pay months into our emergency account. I'll ask my cousin, who works at a nearby packaging plant, to tell me when paid adult setter training is actually offered. If there is a recognized guarded place with fees and paid time covered, I'll attend; if robots later cut my shifts, I'll apply only to posted safe local roles with sufficient regular pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later change, while our own wages look secure now. A decade gives me time to learn with a person beside me rather than a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could your cousin tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin could tell me what the setter actually does on a shift and whether the course ends with a useful certificate. A conversation with my cousin at the packaging plant is not a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a future shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year we would compare the mortgage balance with our real savings and wages. If a new shift clashes with school or later care duties, the posted hours must be workable as well as the pay.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes ordering before robots fold bags around 2039.
A **family contact** may help identify real paid training, not guarantee work.
think: At **56**, I may still need factory wages and a mortgage payment.
Current **two wages** and a decade give planning time despite a small reserve.
do: **Keep** the current bag job and add new wage savings.
**Attend** recognized setter training if real paid guarded place offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local work if later shifts fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots with current wages secure.
S4.quote: A conversation with my cousin at the packaging plant is not a job offer.
fieldNote: Her **traditional outlook** favors paid apprenticeship and family information without assuming a place.
Later **job applications** depend on cut hours, a safe reachable posting and adequate regular pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full bag-line wages after bills
Ask packaging-plant cousin about real paid setter places
Attend recognized setter course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local role if shifts cut, pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because robots around 2031 could reduce the bag-line wage we need for the mortgage. A written crew plan, an offered paid practical apprenticeship and a real safe local factory job at enough pay would help us choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the first bag after a robot changeover can hold the flour it is meant to carry. A sealed paper bag has to hold its weight before a production total means anything.

headlineQuote: A sealed paper bag has to hold its weight before a production total means anything.
portrait: **Sara**, 43, is a junior paper-bag machine operator with secondary school education and typical factory pay.
She and her repair-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with two months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI** and prefers guarded hands-on instruction from an experienced adult.
Her **traditional outlook** favors work, apprenticeships and family advice as robots approach the bag line.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to capable bag-line robots around 2031 before her household can replace that wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, offered paid practical training and posted safe local work at sufficient pay would help.
